 1             Plaintiffs Christine Garcia, R.G., I.G., Billy Ho, and B.H. (“Plaintiffs”), individually and on
 2       behalf of the proposed class defined below, bring this action against Defendant PowerSchool
 3       Holdings, Inc. and Defendant PowerSchool Group LLC (“PowerSchool” or “Defendants”) and
 4       alleges as follows:
 5   I.        SUMMARY OF THE ACTION
 6             1.      PowerSchool is the largest provider of cloud-based education software in the
 7       United States. It is used by more than 18,000 customers, primarily K-12 school districts and
 8       educators, to support more than 50 million students— more than 75% of K-12 students in North
 9       America. As part of its business, PowerSchool maintains in its computer systems the personally
10       identifying information (“PII” or “Private Information”) and/or protected health information
11       (“PHI”) of 60 million people, including teachers, students, and their guardians.
12             2.      Despite holding the highly sensitive personal information of millions of people—
13       many of whom are minors—PowerSchool left gaping cybersecurity holes. Unbeknownst to its
14       end users PowerSchool stored PII and PHI in either unencrypted or inadequately encrypted
15       formats on an Internet-accessible environment that did not support multi-factor authentication
16       and allowed hackers to access and then exfiltrate vast amounts of data from that environment.
17             3.      At some point between December 19 and December 28, 2024, hackers breached
18       the company’s vulnerable systems and exfiltrated the valuable PII and PHI stored within (the
19       “Data Breach” or “Breach”). PowerSchool learned of the Data Breach on December 28, 2024,
20       and began to investigate. Beginning on January 8, 2025, PowerSchool began notifying customers
21       that their data was accessed, and that they were impacted.
22             4.      Now, Plaintiffs and other members of the proposed class must deal with the
23       fallout. The attack exposed over 60 million individuals’ PII and PHI in total. According to public
24       reports, the hacker claimed to have taken data on 62,488,628 students and 9,506,624 teachers
25       in North America. 1 PowerSchool has neither confirmed nor denied the accuracy of these

27       BleepingComputer, January 22, 2025,
         https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/powerschool-hacker-claims-they-stole-data-
28
         of-62-million-students/.

 3          5.      The Private Information stolen in the Data Breach includes dates of birth,
 4   addresses, phone numbers, emails, photo identification, and tax information numbers. The

28   principal place of business at 150 Parkshore Dr., Folsom, California 95630.

 1          13.    Defendant PowerSchool Group LLC is a Delaware Limited Liability Company
 2   with its principal place of business at 150 Parkshore Dr., Folsom, California 95630.
 3          14.    Defendant PowerSchool Holdings, Inc. and PowerSchool Group LLC are
 4   collectively referred to as PowerSchool or Defendants.
 5          15.    At all relevant times, each Defendant was a principal, agent, alter ego, joint
 6   venturer, partner, or affiliate of each other, and in doing the acts alleged herein, was acting
 7   within the course and scope of that principal, agent, alter ego, joint venture, partnership, or
 8   affiliate relationship. Each Defendant had actual knowledge of the wrongful acts of each other;
 9   ratified, approved, joined in, acquiesced, or authorized the wrongful acts of each other; and
10   retained the benefits of those wrongful acts.
11   III.   JURISDICTION AND VENUE
12          16.    This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this matter pursuant to 28 U.S.C.
13   § 1332(d). The amount in controversy in this class action exceeds $5,000,000, exclusive of
14   interest and costs, and there are numerous Class members who are citizens of states other than
15   Defendants’ states of citizenship.
16          17.    This Court has personal jurisdiction over Defendants because they conduct
17   substantial business and have minimum contacts with the State of California.
18          18.    Venue is proper in this District under 28 U.S.C. §1391(b) because a substantial
19   part of the events or omissions giving rise to Plaintiffs’ claims occurred in this District.
20   IV.    FACTUAL BACKGROUND
21          A.     Background on PowerSchool
22          19.    PowerSchool holds itself out “[a]s a leading provider of cloud-based software in
23   North America.” Its product supports vast numbers of teachers, students, and their parents.
24   Seventy-five percent of American school children, over 35 million, use PowerSchool. Over
25   16,000 customers rely on PowerSchool, including 90 of the largest 100 districts by student
26   enrollment.
27          20.    PowerSchool built itself into a market leader in “secure” education technology. It
28   was so successful that in 2024, Bain Capital acquired PowerSchool for $5.6 billion.

 1             21.     The data PowerSchool collects far exceeds traditional education records of school-
 2       age children, including thousands of person-specific data fields.
 3             22.     PowerSchool does not fully disclose what data it collects from school-age children
 4       or their parents.
 5             23.     PowerSchool refuses to provide children and parents access to their data or the
 6       information it generates using that data.
 7             24.     PowerSchool collects and maintains the PHI and PII of customers, including but

13                     e. tax identification number

18                     j. photo identification
19                     k. employment information

21       access rights to children, parental restraining orders, and instructions about when certain
22       students need to take medication. 2

 1         B.      The Data Breach
 2         26.     As of this writing, PowerSchool has provided scant information about what
 3   happened in the data breach – but the available information shows serious gaps in
 4   PowerSchool’s information security controls.
 5         27.     On December 19, 2024, financially motivated hackers used compromised
 6   credentials to access PowerSource, a “community-focused customer portal.” When used
 7   appropriately, PowerSource “is available to all district and school staff, including teachers,
 8   administrators and IT staff.” PowerSchool has admitted that at the time of the data breach,
 9   PowerSource did not support (let alone require) multi-factor authentication, a standard
10   information security control that on its own would have prevented this Data Breach.
11         28.     The hackers then spent the next couple of weeks conducting reconnaissance in the
12   PowerSchool environment. Failing to notice active hacking over weeks indicates that
13   PowerSchool either lacked standard intrusion detection systems adequate to notice this
14   suspicious activity or that PowerSchool personnel failed to heed the warning of their systems. If
15   PowerSchool had properly implemented and configured these standard information security
16   controls, this Data Breach would not have happened or would have been halted before the data
17   was exfiltrated.
18         29.     Moreover, PowerSource was configured to allow users to access the vast array of
19   data that PowerSchool stored in its PowerSchool SIS system. PowerSchool’s marketing

13   their families as it provides the platform families use for online enrollment in its customers’

14   schools and districts.

15         31.     PowerSchool SIS also gathers data on students and families from its customers and

16   their employees, including data on “attendance, behavior, health, graduation tracking, asset

17   tracking, and student demographics.”

18         32.     From a cybersecurity perspective, it is inexcusable that a company would allow

19   access to such sensitive information through an internet-facing portal that is not protected by

20   multi-factor authentication. But PowerSchool’s security failings are far worse than just this.

21         33.     Typically, when hackers are able to use stolen credentials, they are able to get

22   access to whatever data the rightful owner of those credentials would be permitted to see. Here,

23   however, the hackers were able to access the collective data of thousands of different users. This

24   indicates either that PowerSchool’s systems were internally misconfigured to permit

25   dangerously broad access or that PowerSchool failed to prevent the theft of high-level

26   administrative credentials, which should have required multiple security controls to use.

27         34.     On December 22, the hackers used a data export tool normally used for remote

28   support to create and export two massive data files: students_export.csv and teachers_export.csv.

 1   Once again, standard information security controls should have prevented this activity. For
 2   example, PowerSchool should have implemented Data Loss Prevention (DLP) technology that
 3   would have noticed this data aggregation, particularly from so many different customers, and
 4   halted the action. A DLP solution also would have integrated with PowerSource’s intrusion
 5   detection systems to immediately alert information security personnel to the hackers’ presence.
 6   Again, these are standard information security controls that any entity hosting massive quantities
 7   of Private Information should have implemented.
 8         35.    In fact, PowerSchool’s security was so poor that it allowed the hackers to obtain
 9   data from PowerSchool customers that hosted their own data on their own servers around the
10   country. As long as they were using PowerSchool SIS, they were vulnerable.
11         36.    Once the hackers had aggregated millions of records into these two files, they
12   exfiltrated the data without PowerSchool ever noticing such massive data transfers. Properly
13   implemented intrusion detection and DLP tools would have stopped the hackers from obtaining
14   the data files. But PowerSchool’s information security controls again failed.
15         37.    PowerSchool never even learned of the Data Breach until December 28, 2024,
16   when the hackers contacted PowerSchool to seek a ransom in exchange for purportedly deleting
17   the data.
18         38.    PowerSchool investigated the Data Breach and identified the compromised
19   products and customers. It confirmed that the breach affected “families and educators” and
20   various types of sensitive Private Information, including “the individual’s name, contact
